title: Short Stuff: Redacted!
summary: Short Stuff episode on redaction. The hosts open with Halloween banter and a plug for Judge John Hodgman's tour, then define redaction as removing or blacking out sensitive parts of documents. They cover reasons to redact under FOIA, HIPAA, FERPA, court orders, and civil-case discovery (trade secrets, privilege, unrelated CCs). They discuss old-school black marker redaction and the risk that originals can be held up to the light, the Amber Heard/Johnny Depp trial where a redacted original was visible on camera, and attorney Mark Zaid's advice to cut or delete text rather than trust software. They describe the Paul Manifort case, where a Guardian journalist, John Swain, copied text under a black rectangle drawn in Microsoft Word and pasted it out. They close with a guessing-from-redaction-length idea and the moral that redactors must do it right.

segments.title: Halloween banter and Judge John Hodgman tour plug
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Spirit Halloween decorations and a scary toddler prop, then mention the Judge John Hodgman podcast tour.

segments.title: Defining redaction and where it is used
segments.summary: Redaction is defined as removing or blacking out sensitive document content. Examples include FOIA requests, court orders, HIPAA medical privacy, and FERPA education records.

segments.title: Redaction in civil legal discovery
segments.summary: In civil cases, discovery requires sharing documents, which may include copyrighted, trademarked, trade secret, unrelated-party, or privileged material that must be redacted. No single prescribed method exists, and errors can be costly.

segments.title: Black marker redaction and the Amber Heard trial
segments.summary: Black marker on paper is the traditional method, and copies should be made because originals can be read against light. The hosts recall a TV broadcast of the Johnny Depp and Amber Heard trial where a redacted original was visible and its text was readable online.

segments.title: Electronic redaction and attorney Mark Zaid's method
segments.summary: Software overlays can be undone, so attorney Mark Zaid cuts out text with scissors or deletes it and types a replacement such as 'deleted by request of the CIA'.

segments.title: Manafort case and the Guardian's copy-paste failure
segments.summary: In the Paul Manafort case, a Guardian journalist, John Swain, copied text hidden under a black rectangle drawn in Microsoft Word, because the underlying text was not removed. The hosts discuss how such errors come from inexperience.

segments.title: Guessing redacted names from length
segments.summary: Chuck suggests that redacted text length can hint at the hidden content, so redactors might use longer blocks for short names. The hosts joke about made-up names.

segments.title: Consequences of bad redaction
segments.summary: Bad redaction can bring legal penalties, fines a client must pay, loss of trust, and reputational damage. The hosts conclude that redactors should do the job right.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes the short episode and gives the iHeartRadio credit line.
